citation.title: Reform preferences of key actors in the UNFCCC process

question: Which reforms of the COP climate negotiations do state representatives and non-state actors prefer, and where is support broad enough to overcome the consensus rule.
data: Preregistered conjoint survey experiment among COP29 (Baku) participants; data collection completed 5 June 2025. 151 completed responses (63 state representatives, 14.0% response rate; 88 non-state actors, 27.8%); 1,812 profile evaluations. Sampling frame: 449 state representatives (UNFCCC national focal points plus other officials cross-checked against the COP29 attendance list) and 317 non-state actors from the top 10th percentile of delegation size by actor type.
method: Forced-choice conjoint: each respondent chose between two randomly built reform proposals in six tasks, across six attributes (presidency, decision rules, stakeholder representation, observer role, transparency/accountability, implementation focus). Effects reported as average marginal component effects (AMCEs) and marginal means (MMs), standard errors clustered by respondent. Piloted on site at COP29 (17 state responses).

definitions.definition: Mainly UNFCCC national focal points, heads of delegation and other key officials, typically from foreign or environment ministries.
definitions.quote: State representatives in our sample are mainly designated national focal points in the UNFCCC, typically high-level officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or Environment

definitions.definition: Observer organisations in the top 10th percentile of total delegates sent to the meeting, stratified by actor type.
definitions.quote: defined as those in the top 10th percentile of total delegates sent to the meeting, stratified by actor type

definitions.definition: Attribute comparing status quo open participation with a reform that limits fossil-fuel company involvement or one that strengthens support for underrepresented groups. Exact wording is in Table 1, which is not in the extracted text.
definitions.quote: Stakeholder representation compares the status quo of open participation with reforms that either limit fossil-fuel company involvement or strengthen support for underrepresented groups.

proxies.indicator: UNFCCC constituency groups (BINGO, ENGO, RINGO and others) taken from the list of admitted NGO focal points.
proxies.quote: business and industry NGOs (BINGOs; n = 47), environmental NGOs (ENGOs; n = 143)

proxies.concept: presence of a state representative in the national team
proxies.indicator: Registration on the COP29 attendance list, cross-checked against the list of national focal points.
proxies.quote: COP29 participation was used as an inclusion criterion to ensure that all sampled state representatives were members of their country’s negotiation team.

findings.claim: Non-state actors prefer reforms that limit fossil fuel company participation; state representatives are close to indifferent. In the pooled sample the effect is positive but not statistically significant.
findings.quote: non-state actors are more supportive of reforms that limit fossil fuel company participation and expand opportunities for observer engagement.

findings.claim: Non-state actors: limiting fossil fuel participation raised selection by 9.3 percentage points (AMCE 0.093, CI 0.007 to 0.178).
findings.quote: reforms that would limit the participation of fossil fuel companies and associated interests (AMCE 0.093, 95% CI 0.007 to 0.178)
findings.page: Differences between state representatives and non-state actors

findings.claim: In the pooled sample, limiting fossil-fuel participation gives a modest positive but non-significant estimate.
findings.quote: both limiting fossil-fuel participation and increasing support for the underrepresented yield modest positive but non-statistical estimates.
findings.page: Relative support for COP reform proposals

findings.claim: Absolute support (marginal mean) among non-state actors for limiting fossil fuel participation is slightly above 0.5; state representatives are near indifferent.
findings.quote: also lean towards limiting fossil fuel participation (MM 0.542, 95% CI 0.491 to 0.592), whereas state representatives are closer to indifferent on these items.
findings.page: Absolute support for COP reform proposals

findings.claim: The main state versus non-state differences concern observer participation and fossil fuel interests; both groups support transparency and implementation reforms.
findings.quote: the main differences between state representatives and non-state actors concern observer participation and the role of fossil fuel interests
findings.page: Differences between state representatives and non-state actors

findings.claim: Authors suggest participation rules are contested partly because states control accreditation.
findings.quote: participation rules implicate states’ authority over accreditation

findings.claim: Authors argue that reforms to presidency, participation rules and consensus are unlikely to advance without coalition-building (an interpretation and recommendation, not a measured result).
findings.quote: reforms to the COP presidency, participation rules and consensus-based decision-making remain more contested and are unlikely to move forward without sustained coalition-building.

limitations.point: Small, non-representative elite sample with low response rate among state representatives; non-response could bias results.
limitations.quote: If individuals who chose not to participate systematically differ in their reform preferences from those who did respond, this could bias the estimated levels of support for some reform proposals.

limitations.point: Overrepresentation of Europe-based, mostly NGO, non-state respondents.
limitations.quote: the sample includes a relatively large share of Europe-based respondents among non-state actors and cannot be treated as statistically representative of all COP participants.

limitations.point: Regional groupings only: no distinction between country coalitions, and no question on country of origin, so EU member state delegations cannot be isolated.
limitations.quote: focusing on regional groupings prevents differentiation between state actors from distinct party coalitions, limiting insight into power asymmetries in support for specific proposals.

limitations.point: Forced-choice design measures relative preference, not standalone endorsement of any reform.
limitations.quote: a forced-choice conjoint captures relative preferences rather than absolute endorsement.

limitations.point: The study measures stated preferences about reforms. It does not count or classify fossil fuel-linked delegates or business presence in delegations, and defines no fossil fuel-linked category. Table 1 (exact wording of attribute levels), Extended Data tables and Supplementary Information are not in the extracted text.
Peer review status is not stated in the extracted text (published in Nature Climate Change; ledger left it blank).
